summary: This standards-track document specifies Mobile IPv6, which lets a node stay reachable while moving. A mobile node keeps a home address and gets a care-of address where it currently is. A home agent forwards traffic between them.

plainLanguage.summary: Mobile IPv6 lets a device keep its home address when it connects to a different network. A home agent can forward its packets to its current address, or a correspondent can learn that address and send directly. This helps existing network connections continue across a move.

questions: what is the return routability procedure
subtitle: How an IPv6 device keeps one permanent address and stays reachable while it moves between networks.

tldr.problem: When a device moves to another network, its IP address normally changes. Connections that rely on the old address can then stop working.
tldr.mechanism: Mobile IPv6 gives the device a permanent home address and a care-of address for its current network. A home agent forwards packets between those addresses, while route optimization lets a correspondent send directly to the care-of address.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6275 is a Proposed Standard that revises and obsoletes RFC 3775. It defines both forwarding through a home agent and direct delivery after a correspondent accepts a binding.

today: RFC 6275 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2011. It obsoletes RFC 3775.

sections.title: Why IPv6 Needs Mobility Support
sections.content:
Without mobility support, packets sent to a device's home address cannot reach it after it leaves its home link. The device could use a new IP address on each link, but connections that use its old address could not continue unchanged.

Mobile IPv6 addresses this at the network layer. The mobile node keeps its home address as it moves, so transport protocols and applications can continue to use that address. The protocol supports movement between similar or different link types.

The RFC does not cover every mobility problem. It excludes, among other things, access control on a visited link, mobile routers, local mobility management, and distinguishing packet loss from bit errors. It obsoletes RFC 3775 after issues were found during integration, testing, and deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: Mobile IPv6 lets a device keep the same home address when it changes networks. This means applications can keep using that address while the network redirects packets to the device's current location.

sections.title: Home Addresses, Care-of Addresses and Bindings
sections.content:
A mobile node is a device that can change its network attachment and remain reachable through its home address. Its home address is assigned within its home link. When the device visits another link, it can also use a care-of address with that link's subnet prefix.

A binding associates a home address with a care-of address for a stated lifetime. The mobile node registers its primary care-of address with a home agent, a router on the home link. A correspondent node is any peer communicating with the mobile node; it may be stationary or mobile.

Home agents and correspondent nodes keep a Binding Cache of bindings for other nodes. The mobile node keeps a Binding Update List of bindings it has established or is trying to establish. Home and care-of addresses must be unicast routable addresses. The RFC says unique-local addresses should not be used for them when other choices are available.
sections.plainLanguage: The home address identifies the device even when it moves. A care-of address identifies where it can receive packets now, and a binding links the two addresses for a limited time.

sections.title: Two Ways to Deliver Packets
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 supports bidirectional tunneling and route optimization. With bidirectional tunneling, the correspondent does not need Mobile IPv6 support or a registered binding. Packets for the mobile node go to its home agent, which tunnels them to the primary care-of address. In the other direction, the mobile node tunnels packets through the home agent before they travel to the correspondent.

Route optimization requires the mobile node to register its binding with the correspondent. The correspondent can then send packets directly to the care-of address using a type 2 routing header that carries the home address. For packets in the other direction, the mobile node uses its care-of address in the IPv6 header and carries its home address in a Home Address destination option.

The home and care-of addresses let higher protocol layers continue to use the home address. The direct route can be shorter and avoids congestion at the home agent and home link. The tunneled route remains available when there is no correspondent binding.
sections.plainLanguage: Without a registered binding, packets travel through the home agent, which forwards them to the device. With route optimization, a correspondent that has accepted the device's binding can send packets directly to its current address.

sections.title: Movement, Registration and Returning Home
sections.content:
The mobile node detects a network-layer move using IPv6 Neighbor Discovery, including Router Discovery and Neighbor Unreachability Detection. It then forms a care-of address, registers its primary care-of address with the home agent, and updates correspondent nodes with which it uses route optimization. The RFC advises avoiding a move to a new default router until the current router is no longer reachable when possible.

For a home registration, the mobile node sends a Binding Update with the Home Registration and Acknowledge bits set. The home agent checks and authenticates the update, performs Duplicate Address Detection when required, and returns a Binding Acknowledgement. It then advertises the mobile node's home address on the home link and answers Neighbor Solicitations as a proxy, so packets for that address reach the home agent and can be tunneled to the mobile node.

When the mobile node returns to its home link, it must deregister before using its home address there. It sends a Binding Update with a zero lifetime and its home address as the care-of address. The home agent then stops intercepting packets for it.
sections.plainLanguage: After detecting a move, the device gets a care-of address and tells its home agent where to forward packets. When it returns home, it sends a zero-lifetime update so the agent stops forwarding those packets.

sections.title: Mobility Messages and Binding Updates
sections.content:
The Mobility Header is an IPv6 extension header for messages that create and manage bindings. IPv6 identifies it with Next Header value 135. Its fields identify the following protocol, the header length and message type, and include a reserved field and checksum; message-specific data follows. The header length is a multiple of 8 octets, and receivers must skip mobility options they do not understand.

The defined message types include Home Test Init and Care-of Test Init, their replies, Binding Update, Binding Acknowledgement, Binding Refresh Request, and Binding Error. A Binding Update tells a home agent or correspondent about a binding. It carries a sequence number, flags, and a lifetime; each lifetime unit is 4 seconds, and a lifetime of zero requests deletion of the binding.

A Binding Acknowledgement reports whether an update was accepted or rejected and returns the sequence number. The Binding Error reports certain mobility-related errors, including use of a Home Address option when the receiver has no matching binding.
sections.plainLanguage: The Mobility Header carries messages that set up, refresh, or remove address bindings. A Binding Update gives a node the new address and how long the binding should last; a zero lifetime asks the receiver to delete it.

sections.title: Authorizing Updates to Home Agents and Peers
sections.content:
A mobile node and its home agent must protect Binding Updates and Acknowledgements with an IPsec security association that provides integrity and authenticity. The home agent checks that the home address matches the security association, preventing a node from registering on behalf of another mobile node. Manual security associations must be supported; IKEv2 may be supported for automatic key management.

A correspondent node usually has no prearranged security association with the mobile node. Instead, the return routability procedure checks that the mobile node can receive messages at both its home address and care-of address. The node sends a Home Test Init through the home agent and a Care-of Test Init directly. The correspondent returns a separate token along each path.

The mobile node combines the two tokens into a binding management key and uses it to authenticate its Binding Update. The correspondent can verify the update without keeping per-node state during the tests. Bindings authorized this way must not last longer than 420 seconds. If return-routability signaling repeatedly fails, the mobile node must fall back to sending through its home agent.
sections.plainLanguage: The home agent accepts updates protected by a shared IPsec security association. A correspondent checks that the device can receive messages at both addresses before accepting a direct-route update.

sections.title: Neighbor Discovery and Home Network Information
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 adds information to IPv6 Router Advertisements. A Home Agent bit identifies a router acting as a home agent on that link. A Router Address bit lets a router advertise its global address, which helps build the list used for home-agent discovery.

Two new Neighbor Discovery options provide more information. The Advertisement Interval option tells a mobile node how often to expect unsolicited Router Advertisements, which can help it detect movement. The Home Agent Information option provides a preference and lifetime for ordering home agents in a discovery reply.

The RFC also defines ICMP messages for discovering home agents and for requesting or advertising home-network prefixes. Dynamic home-agent address discovery has no security protection in this specification; the RFC describes it as intended for deployments where security is not needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can advertise whether they are home agents and provide information that helps a moving device notice a network change. A device can also request home-agent or home-prefix information, but the defined home-agent discovery exchange has no security protection.

sections.title: Security Protections and Their Limits
sections.content:
The main threat is a false binding: an attacker could claim that a mobile node is at the wrong address and redirect traffic. This can expose or disrupt traffic, impersonate a node, or send unwanted traffic to a victim. The RFC also discusses replayed updates, forged tunnel packets, reflection attacks, and routing loops involving multiple home agents.

IPsec protects home registrations. Return routability limits correspondent updates to a mobile node that can receive probes at both claimed addresses, while sequence numbers and message authentication protect updates from replay and modification. Restrictions on the Home Address option, type 2 routing header, and tunnel addresses address other identified attacks.

Return routability does not protect against an attacker who can monitor the path between the home agent and correspondent. The RFC limits the lifetime of bindings created through this procedure to 420 seconds. It also provides no security mechanism for dynamic home-agent address discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: Security checks make it harder to redirect a device's traffic with a false address update. They do not stop an attacker who can monitor the path between the home agent and correspondent, and home-agent discovery is unprotected.
